clinicalPearls: A common viral illness of young children, typically 6 months to 3 years, most often caused by parainfluenza viruses, producing upper airway obstruction at the subglottis.
Characterised by a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, usually preceded by coryza and worse at night.
Diagnosis is clinical; a frontal neck radiograph may show subglottic narrowing (the steeple sign) but is not required.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay and benefit essentially all severities, reducing symptoms and the need for further intervention.
Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides rapid, temporary relief in moderate to severe cases and mandates a period of observation for rebound.
Keeping the child calm and comfortable is important, as agitation and crying worsen airway obstruction.
Stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxaemia indicates significant obstruction requiring active treatment.
Consider alternative diagnoses when the presentation is atypical: sudden toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis, and drooling with dysphagia is a warning sign.
reference.pathophysiology: Viral infection produces inflammation and oedema of the larynx, trachea, and subglottic tissues. Because the subglottis is the narrowest part of a child's airway and is encircled by rigid cricoid cartilage, even modest mucosal swelling markedly narrows the lumen, dramatically increasing airway resistance and producing turbulent airflow heard as inspiratory stridor and the characteristic barking cough. Increased work of breathing follows, and severe obstruction can cause hypoxaemia and fatigue.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical severity assessment (e.g. presence of stridor at rest and recession)
Anteroposterior neck radiograph only if diagnosis is uncertain (steeple sign)
Avoid interventions that distress the child until the airway is secured in severe cases
redFlags: Stridor at rest with marked chest wall recession
Cyanosis, hypoxaemia, or altered mental status / lethargy
Drooling, dysphagia, or a toxic-appearing child suggesting epiglottitis
Rapidly worsening obstruction or exhaustion despite treatment
Biphasic stridor indicating severe fixed obstruction
reference.prognosis: Most children have mild, self-limiting illness that resolves within a few days; severe airway compromise is uncommon and the need for intubation is rare with appropriate treatment.
pitfalls: Distressing the child with unnecessary examination or procedures, worsening obstruction
Withholding corticosteroids in mild cases where they still provide benefit
Discharging a child after nebulised adrenaline without an adequate observation period for rebound
Failing to recognise epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis presenting with a croup-like picture
management: Give a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone (or prednisolone) to essentially all children regardless of severity, as the mainstay reducing symptoms and need for further intervention
Administer nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) for moderate to severe disease to achieve rapid temporary relief, followed by a period of observation for rebound
Keep the child calm and comfortable, minimising distress since agitation and crying worsen airway obstruction
Provide supportive care with supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia and attention to hydration
In severe or impending airway obstruction, summon senior anaesthetic and ENT support and secure the airway, with intubation reserved for the rare refractory case
Give safety-netting and discharge advice and observe adequately after nebulised adrenaline before discharge
